claim: Four orthologous fluorescent proteins (avGFP, amacGFP, cgreGFP, and ppluGFP2) were characterized with a broad range of sequence divergence.
source: We characterized the fitness peaks of four orthologous fluorescent proteins with a broad range of sequence divergence.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the study characterized four orthologous fluorescent proteins with varying sequence divergence.

claim: Two of the four studied fitness peaks were sharp.
source: While two of the four studied fitness peaks were sharp, the other two were considerably flatter, being almost entirely free of epistatic interactions.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding from the experimental data.

claim: Two of the four studied fitness peaks were considerably flatter and almost entirely free of epistatic interactions.
source: While two of the four studied fitness peaks were sharp, the other two were considerably flatter, being almost entirely free of epistatic interactions.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding from the experimental data.

claim: Mutationally robust proteins with flat fitness peaks were not optimal templates for machine-learning-driven protein design.
source: Mutationally robust proteins, characterized by a flat fitness peak, were not optimal templates for machine-learning-driven protein design – instead, predictions were more accurate for fragile proteins with epistatic landscapes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the machine learning prediction experiments.

claim: Predictions were more accurate for fragile proteins with epistatic landscapes.
source: Mutationally robust proteins, characterized by a flat fitness peak, were not optimal templates for machine-learning-driven protein design – instead, predictions were more accurate for fragile proteins with epistatic landscapes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the machine learning prediction experiments.

claim: The fitness landscape is often conceptualized as a multidimensional surface.
source: The fitness landscape is often conceptualised as a multidimensional surface (de Visser and Krug, 2014; Ferretti et al., 2018; Kondrashov and Kondrashov, 2015; Wright, 1932) with one dimension representing fitness, or another phenotype, and the other dimensions each representing a genotype's locus.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The fitness landscape concept was originally introduced to describe the relationship between fitness and the entire genome.
source: Originally, the fitness landscape was introduced to describe the relationship between fitness and the entire genome (de Visser and Krug, 2014; Wright, 1932).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational literature.

claim: The fitness landscape concept has been adapted to describe the relationship between protein function and its protein-coding gene sequence.
source: Over time, the usefulness of the concept of the fitness landscape led to the adaptation of this term to describe the relationship between protein function and its protein-coding gene sequence (Biswas et al., 2021; Ogden et al., 2019; Romero and Arnold, 2009; Wittmann et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: GFP is approximately 250 amino acids long.
source: Even for the Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP), which is only ~250 amino acids long, there are 20250 possible genotypes.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about GFP structure.

claim: There are 20^250 possible genotypes for GFP.
source: Even for the Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP), which is only ~250 amino acids long, there are 20250 possible genotypes.
evidence: This is a mathematical calculation based on the number of amino acids and positions.

claim: Without complex epistatic interactions, the fitness landscape could be deduced from the independent contribution of each amino acid at each site, requiring just 5000 measurements for GFP.
source: Without complex epistatic interactions between amino acid sites the fitness landscape could be deduced from the independent contribution of each amino acid at each site (Kondrashov and Kondrashov, 2015), requiring just 5000 (20*250) measurements of the effects of all single mutations in GFP.
evidence: This is a theoretical calculation supported by citation.

claim: Epistatic interactions between amino acid sites are common.
source: However, epistatic interactions between amino acid sites are common (Russ et al., 2020) and many of them are too complex to predict with available data (Pokusaeva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature.

claim: Many epistatic interactions are too complex to predict with available data.
source: However, epistatic interactions between amino acid sites are common (Russ et al., 2020) and many of them are too complex to predict with available data (Pokusaeva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature.

claim: Each extant genotype is a point of high fitness, or a fitness peak, on the genotype space.
source: Each extant genotype, one that is found in an extant species, is a point of high fitness, or a fitness peak, on the highly dimensional and extraordinarily large genotype space (de Visser and Krug, 2014; Fragata et al., 2019; Smith, 1970; Wright, 1932).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to foundational literature.

claim: Extant genotypes must be connected by ridges of high fitness because they had a common ancestor.
source: These extant genotypes had a common ancestor, so they must be connected by ridges of high fitness (Gong et al., 2013; Smith, 1970; Povolotskaya and Kondrashov, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference from evolutionary theory supported by citations.

claim: Only an infinitesimally small fraction of all genotypes are functional (fewer than 10^-11).
source: Nevertheless, only an infinitesimally small fraction of all genotypes are functional (fewer than 10–11), those that correspond to fitness peaks and ridges, and the remaining genotypes confer low fitness (Keefe and Szostak, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental literature.

claim: Fitness peaks are sharp.
source: The fitness peaks are sharp (Bank et al., 2015; Melamed et al., 2013; Sarkisyan et al., 2016) and the ridges are narrow (Gong et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2017; Pokusaeva et al., 2019; Sailer et al., 2020) and, on average, only a few random mutations in a wildtype sequence reduce its fitness to zero (Hartman and Tullman-Ercek, 2019; Kemble et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental literature.

claim: The ridges connecting fitness peaks are narrow.
source: The fitness peaks are sharp (Bank et al., 2015; Melamed et al., 2013; Sarkisyan et al., 2016) and the ridges are narrow (Gong et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2017; Pokusaeva et al., 2019; Sailer et al., 2020) and, on average, only a few random mutations in a wildtype sequence reduce its fitness to zero (Hartman and Tullman-Ercek, 2019; Kemble et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental literature.

claim: On average, only a few random mutations in a wildtype sequence reduce its fitness to zero.
source: The fitness peaks are sharp (Bank et al., 2015; Melamed et al., 2013; Sarkisyan et al., 2016) and the ridges are narrow (Gong et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2017; Pokusaeva et al., 2019; Sailer et al., 2020) and, on average, only a few random mutations in a wildtype sequence reduce its fitness to zero (Hartman and Tullman-Ercek, 2019; Kemble et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: The sharpness of fitness peaks is enhanced by negative epistasis.
source: The sharpness of the peaks is enhanced by negative epistasis, such that a genotype with several random mutations has a lower fitness than expected if mutations acted independently (Haddox et al., 2018; Sarkisyan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: cgreGFP has 59% sequence divergence from avGFP.
source: To complement the available data on the avGFP fitness peak (Sarkisyan et al., 2016; GFP from Aequorea victoria, Hydrozoa), we experimentally characterized three additional GFP sequences, each with a different degree of sequence divergence from avGFP: amacGFP (Aequorea macrodactyla, Hydrozoa), cgreGFP (Clytia gregaria, Hydrozoa), and ppluGPF2 (Pontellina plumata, Copepoda), with 18%, 59%, and 82% sequence divergence, respectively (Figure 1b; Table 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states the sequence divergence percentages, and Figure 1b displays this information.

claim: ppluGFP2 has 82% sequence divergence from avGFP.
source: To complement the available data on the avGFP fitness peak (Sarkisyan et al., 2016; GFP from Aequorea victoria, Hydrozoa), we experimentally characterized three additional GFP sequences, each with a different degree of sequence divergence from avGFP: amacGFP (Aequorea macrodactyla, Hydrozoa), cgreGFP (Clytia gregaria, Hydrozoa), and ppluGPF2 (Pontellina plumata, Copepoda), with 18%, 59%, and 82% sequence divergence, respectively (Figure 1b; Table 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states the sequence divergence percentages, and Figure 1b displays this information.

claim: The new dataset contained 25,000-35,000 genotypes per each of the three additional fitness peaks.
source: The new dataset contained 25,000–35,000 genotypes per each of the three additional fitness peaks, with each mutant genotype harboring on average 3–4 mutations relative to its respective wildtype sequence (Table 1).
evidence: The text states this and Table 1 provides the specific numbers.

claim: Each mutant genotype harbored on average 3-4 mutations relative to its respective wildtype sequence.
source: The new dataset contained 25,000–35,000 genotypes per each of the three additional fitness peaks, with each mutant genotype harboring on average 3–4 mutations relative to its respective wildtype sequence (Table 1).

evidence: The text states this finding and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows the data.

evidence: The text states this and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 shows the data.

claim: Mutations of buried amino acid residues had a stronger effect than mutations of residues on the protein surface.

Fitness peaks of most single-mutation neighbours with high levels of fluorescence were sharper than the respective wildtype fitness peaks (Figure 3c), suggesting a local optimization of robustness of each wildtype sequence (Draghi et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2020; Draghi et al., 2010).

claim: For genotypes with 48 mutations (>20% sequence divergence of GFP), predictions had an 8% accuracy when using data for the mutationally robust ppluGFP2 and a 50-60% accuracy for the mutationally fragile cgreGFP.

claim: Individual mutations which were strongly deleterious in some genetic contexts were successfully incorporated into functional predictions.
source: However, three lines of evidence show that our high rate of prediction cannot be explained by universally neutral mutations (also see Poelwijk et al., 2019). First, individual mutations which were strongly deleterious in some genetic contexts were successfully incorporated into functional predictions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), and these conditionally deleterious mutations comprised a significant fraction of all mutations used in predictions, particularly in the case of the epistatic cgreGFP protein (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text states this finding and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 shows the data.

claim: When the goal is to discover as many distant functional proteins as possible, it may be better to select a fragile protein as the original template for a mutational scan.
source: When the goal is to discover as many distant functional proteins as possible (i.e. Bryant et al., 2021; Romero and Arnold, 2009; Russ et al., 2020; Wittmann et al., 2021) it may seem natural to select a structurally or mutationally robust protein. Indeed, a robust protein, one that is known to be able to maintain function upon the introduction of many mutations, seems a good starting point to introduce even more mutations. Our results counter this intuition, and our recommendation is to select a fragile protein as the original template for a mutational scan.
evidence: The text presents this as a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: For the data of the fitness landscape to be useful for a downstream model to predict distant sequences, it has to contain information about epistatic interactions between mutations.
